content_html:
Why the Audience Drives Every Device Decision

Choosing a digital device is not just about picking the newest or cheapest option. Every digital communication needs to reach a specific audience — and that audience has needs, preferences and constraints that determine which device and channel will actually work for them. The spec area covered by this lesson appears directly in Section B scenario questions, where you are asked to recommend a device and justify your choice for a named audience. Getting this right requires a two-step move: identify the audience characteristic, then link it to the specific device or channel feature that addresses it.

Digital Devices — Five Types to Know

The five digital devices in the specification are: smartphone, smartboard, PC/laptop, tablet and smart TV.

A smartphone is the most portable and personal device. It is always connected, fits in a pocket and is operated by touch. It is ideal for reaching individuals on the move — delivery notifications, banking alerts, social media campaigns targeting commuters. Its small screen limits complex data presentation, and it requires mobile-optimised content. A tablet offers a larger touchscreen than a phone without the full keyboard of a laptop. It suits media consumption, educational apps for children, and front-of-house uses such as restaurant ordering systems or museum interactive exhibits. A PC or laptop is the standard device for productivity-focused, data-heavy tasks: managing spreadsheets, writing long documents or running complex software. Users expect keyboard and mouse input, multi-window workflows and full-featured applications. A smartboard is designed for group use from a distance. It is fixed to a wall or stand, uses touch or stylus interaction, and must display content that is large enough to read across a room. It is best suited to classroom teaching, boardroom presentations and collaborative group workshops. A smart TV is designed for passive consumption at distance — video content, streaming services, and in some contexts public information displays. Interaction is typically via remote control or voice, not touch.

Smartphone: advantages — portable, always connected, push notifications reach users instantly, wide adoption. Disadvantages — small screen limits complex content, requires mobile-specific design, may be distracting in formal settings.

Tablet: advantages — larger screen than smartphone, portable, touch-operated, good for visual or interactive content. Disadvantages — less portable than a phone, limited productivity for text-heavy tasks, battery life varies.

PC/laptop: advantages — large screen, full keyboard and mouse, powerful for complex tasks. Disadvantages — less portable, not suitable for on-the-move contexts, requires a desk or stable surface.

Smartboard: advantages — large group-visible display, supports collaborative annotation, good for educational and boardroom settings. Disadvantages — fixed in location, expensive, requires the audience to be physically present.

Smart TV: advantages — large display for shared viewing, familiar to most households, suitable for video-based communications. Disadvantages — limited interactivity, remote control input is imprecise, not suitable for data-heavy or text-heavy content.

Audience Demographics — Four Factors

The spec requires you to assess device and channel suitability against four audience demographic factors: accessibility, age, gender and location.

Key Fact

The four audience demographics are: accessibility (motor, visual, hearing and cognitive needs), age (children, working adults, older adults), gender (design, language and platform preferences may vary), location (urban vs rural broadband, regional device ownership patterns). Always link the demographic to a specific design or device feature in your answer.

Accessibility

Accessibility covers four types of need. Motor accessibility affects how a person physically operates a device — someone with limited hand mobility may struggle with small touchscreen tap targets and benefit from a voice-controlled interface or large-button keyboard. Visual accessibility affects how a person sees the screen — someone with low vision needs large text, high contrast colours and screen-reader compatibility. This affects device choice (a large monitor over a small phone screen) and channel choice (a website with adjustable text size over a fixed-format PDF). Hearing accessibility affects audio-based content — a video delivered via smart TV needs subtitles or captions for deaf or hard-of-hearing users; a VoIP call is unsuitable for someone who cannot hear clearly. Cognitive accessibility affects how easily a person understands and navigates content — complex menus, long paragraphs and jargon-heavy text may be barriers for users with learning difficulties or limited IT literacy.

Age

Younger children are typically tablet users — the larger touch targets and simplified app interfaces on tablets suit developing motor skills, and tablets are common in primary school classrooms. Teenagers and young adults are predominantly smartphone users with high digital literacy. Working adults use a mix of PC/laptop (workplace productivity) and smartphone (personal communication). Older adults may have lower digital literacy, prefer larger text and simpler navigation, and be less likely to have high-speed home broadband — a phone call or printed material may sometimes be more accessible than a digital channel for this demographic.

Gender and Location

Gender demographics can influence platform preferences and design choices, though these vary widely and must not be over-generalised. In the exam, reference to gender demographics is typically about ensuring a design does not inadvertently exclude or alienate a portion of the audience — for example, using inclusive imagery and neutral language. Location is a more concrete demographic factor: urban users typically have access to high-speed broadband and 4G or 5G mobile coverage, making data-heavy channels (HD video streaming, large web applications) viable. Rural users may have slower or more limited connectivity, making lightweight channels — email, SMS-based messaging, or downloadable content that works offline — more reliable choices.

Scenario: A national charity wants to promote a fundraising campaign to retired adults aged 65+ across rural areas. Which device and distribution channel would you recommend?

Device: A PC or laptop, or a large-screen smart TV, would be more suitable than a smartphone. Older adults are less likely to own a smartphone and may have reduced motor dexterity making small touch targets difficult. A TV screen is familiar to this demographic and requires only remote control interaction. Channel: Email is a strong choice because it works on slow broadband connections (rural location), is widely used by retired adults who may check email on a PC, does not require app installation and can include large-text formatted content. A mobile app would be a poor choice — lower smartphone ownership in this demographic, potential difficulty installing and navigating apps.

The exam-scoring move is always the same: state the demographic characteristic → link it to a device or channel feature → explain why that match is suitable (or why the alternative is unsuitable). A one-word answer such as “email” without justification scores zero on a 3-mark question.

Key Fact

The scoring pattern for device/channel recommendation questions is: audience characteristic → device/channel feature → justification. For example: “The audience is older adults with reduced motor dexterity [demographic] — a smart TV with remote control interaction is suitable [device] because it avoids small tap targets that are difficult to use accurately [justification].”
exam_tip_html: Section B scenarios require you to recommend a device and channel for a specific audience. The most common examiner complaint is that students describe what a device is rather than why it suits the audience. Structure every recommendation as: demographic factor → device or channel feature → explanation of why this suits the audience. For example: “The audience is rural adults [location demographic] — email is a suitable distribution channel [channel] because it works on slow broadband connections that are common in rural areas and does not require a high-speed connection to receive [justification].” Answers that just say “email is fast and easy to use” without referencing the demographic will score poorly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five digital devices are smartphone, smart TV, PC/laptop, tablet and smartboard — each has a specific use context, interaction method and audience fit that must be matched to the scenario in the exam.
  • The four audience demographic factors are accessibility (motor, visual, hearing, cognitive), age, gender and location — each directly affects which device and distribution channel is most suitable.
  • Every device or channel recommendation must follow the scoring pattern: demographic characteristic → device or channel feature → justification. Naming the device without linking it to the audience characteristic scores only partial marks.

practice_questions.text: Which digital device is best suited to group viewing across a room in a classroom setting, where all participants must be able to see the content simultaneously?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: smartboard (only). Distractors: smartphone (small screen, individual use), tablet (small screen, individual use), PC/laptop (typically single-user, screen not large enough for group viewing across a room).

practice_questions.text: Identify one accessibility need that would make a smartphone an unsuitable device for a user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one valid accessibility need correctly linked to smartphone limitations, e.g. reduced motor dexterity or motor impairment making small tap targets on a touchscreen difficult to use accurately (1); OR visual impairment meaning the small smartphone screen and text are hard to read even with zoom (1); OR cognitive accessibility needs meaning the complexity of smartphone apps and notifications is overwhelming (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline why location is an important audience demographic when choosing a distribution channel for a digital communication.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: urban audiences typically have access to fast broadband and 4G/5G mobile coverage, making data-heavy channels such as HD video streaming viable (1); rural audiences may have slower or less reliable connectivity, so lightweight channels such as email or SMS that function on low-bandwidth connections are more suitable to ensure the communication can actually be received (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how age as an audience demographic affects the choice of digital device for a campaign targeting primary school children.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: primary school children (typically aged 4–11) are developing motor skills and have lower dexterity than adults (1); tablets are more suitable than smartphones because the larger screen and bigger touch targets are easier to use accurately, and tablets are commonly used in primary education — children are already familiar with them as learning tools (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a national health charity should use email rather than a mobile app to distribute health information to retired adults aged over 70 in rural areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): demographic identified: the target audience is older adults in rural areas (1); email is suitable because it works on slow broadband connections common in rural areas — the charity cannot assume its audience has high-speed internet (1); additionally, older adults are less likely to own smartphones and may have difficulty installing and navigating apps, whereas email is accessible on a PC or laptop which this demographic is more likely to use and be familiar with (1).
Secure (2): two mark points addressed; one demographic factor linked to channel suitability.
Developing (1): email recommended without linking to demographic characteristics or connectivity constraints.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A local council wants to promote a new recycling scheme to three different audience groups: (1) teenagers aged 13–18 in an urban area, (2) adults aged 60+ in a rural area, and (3) users who are visually impaired. For each group, recommend a suitable digital device and distribution channel. Sketch a matrix showing your recommendations and justifications for each group and demographic factor.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): three groups addressed with device, channel and justification all linked to demographic characteristics. Teenagers/urban: smartphone and mobile app or social media channel — high smartphone ownership, urban 4G coverage, young demographic digitally confident (3); adults 60+/rural: PC/laptop and email — lower smartphone ownership in older demographic, email familiar to this age group on desktop, works on slow rural broadband, large text possible in email client (3); visually impaired users: PC/laptop or tablet and website with accessibility features (screen reader compatibility, adjustable text, high contrast) — larger screen aids low-vision users, desktop screen readers work on websites, email also acceptable if formatted for accessibility (3).
Secure (5–7): all three groups addressed with mostly accurate justifications; one or two demographic links missing.
Developing (3–4): two groups addressed with justification, or three groups without demographic linkage.
Emerging (1–2): one group addressed or devices named without justification.
0: no creditworthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: Which digital device is specifically designed for group viewing from a distance, such as in a classroom or boardroom?
Which audience demographic factor relates to the speed and availability of internet connections in different areas?
A user with reduced motor dexterity may find a smartphone difficult to use because the _____ on the touchscreen are too small to press accurately.
The four audience demographic factors that must be considered when selecting a device and channel are accessibility, age, gender and _____.
Match each digital device to its most suitable use context.
right: Shared video viewing in a home or public setting
Interactive group presentations in classrooms or boardrooms
Portable individual device for consuming media and light productivity
On-the-move personal communication and app use

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five digital devices in the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Smartphone, smart TV, PC/laptop, tablet, smartboard.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a tablet often chosen for young children over a smartphone?
flashcard_questions.a: Larger screen and bigger touch targets suit developing motor skills.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four audience demographic factors.
Why is location an important demographic for channel choice?
flashcard_questions.a: Rural areas may have slow connectivity — lightweight channels like email are more reliable than HD video.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of a motor accessibility need.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduced hand mobility making small touchscreen tap targets difficult to press accurately.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of a visual accessibility need.
flashcard_questions.a: Low vision requiring large text, high contrast colours and screen reader support.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might email be preferred over a mobile app for older rural adults?
flashcard_questions.a: Lower smartphone ownership, works on slow broadband, accessible on familiar PC/laptop.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the scoring pattern for device/channel recommendation questions?
Why is a smartboard unsuitable for reaching a geographically dispersed audience?
flashcard_questions.a: It is fixed in one location — the audience must be physically present.

flashcard_questions.q: What visual accessibility feature makes a website more suitable than a fixed PDF?
flashcard_questions.a: Adjustable text size and screen reader compatibility.

flashcard_questions.q: Which device is best for a data-heavy task like managing complex spreadsheets?
flashcard_questions.a: PC/laptop — full keyboard and mouse, large screen, powerful software support.

glossary_terms.definition: A handheld mobile device that combines phone, internet access and app functionality; typically 5–7 inches, always connected, touch-operated.
A large-screen interactive display (typically 55–86 inches) mounted on a wall or stand, designed for group presentations and collaborative use in classrooms or boardrooms.
A personal computer or laptop; a desktop or portable device with a full-size keyboard, mouse and screen, optimised for productivity, data entry and complex software tasks.
A portable touchscreen device larger than a phone (typically 7–13 inches) but smaller than a laptop; suited to media consumption, creative tasks and light productivity on the go.
A large-screen television set with internet connectivity, app support and, in some models, voice or remote control interaction.
Accessibility needs relating to physical, visual, hearing or cognitive differences that affect how a person can interact with a digital device or interface.
The age group of the target audience, which affects device familiarity, physical dexterity, content preferences and typical patterns of device ownership.
The geographical location of the audience, including whether they are urban or rural, which affects internet connectivity, device availability and channel reach.
